a-real-version-of-the-board.description: Anthropic's lead agent gave its subagents vague task descriptions, and they duplicated each other's searches and left gaps until each task carried an objective, an output format, tool guidance and boundaries; one team's account of its own system, not a controlled comparison [1].

everyone-delivered.title: Everyone delivered
everyone-delivered.script: Now the day arrives, and every one of the four has done exactly what was asked. Activities booked a team-building event, Travel arranged how everyone gets there, Venue found a place, and Food and drinks ordered dinner. Each card is ticked, and each freelancer met their own goal perfectly.

none-of-it-adds-up.title: None of it adds up
none-of-it-adds-up.script: And still the party fails, because the failures sit between the cards. Activities booked paintball, while Travel had booked an accessible bus for ten colleagues in wheelchairs, who now sit it out. Travel had everyone carpool, while Food and drinks booked an open bar until one in the morning, so the drivers have been drinking. Venue found a scenic alpine hut, while the guest info from Travel gives only route and times, so people arrive in summer clothes for six degrees at night. And dinner was ordered with 31 vegetarian, which the hut's kitchen reads the Western way, so egg dishes land in front of colleagues who cannot eat them. Every step was perfect, and perfect steps do not add up on their own.

your-question.title: Your question
your-question.script: So here is the question, and I want you to keep it in your head for the whole Episode. What do you, as the manager, need to do so the result still comes out great? One tempting answer is to get the four talking, to hold more meetings. I will leave the question open for now, and we will answer it step by step, from different angles, until we collect the answers at the end.
